reference.source: Weedon's Skin Pathology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A cutaneous deposition disorder characterised by translucent, amber or flesh-coloured dome-shaped papules containing gelatinous colloid material in the dermis
The classic adult form arises on chronically sun-exposed skin, particularly the face, ears, dorsal hands and neck, on a background of marked actinic damage
A rare juvenile form appears before puberty, may be familial, and is thought to derive from degeneration of keratinocytes rather than from actinic elastosis
A pigmented variant is associated with the use of hydroquinone-containing skin-lightening creams and overlaps with exogenous ochronosis
Lesions are usually asymptomatic and cosmetic, and expressing a papule may yield a jelly-like colloid substance
Histology shows fissured, homogeneous eosinophilic colloid masses filling the papillary dermis, with a characteristic clefting artefact and adjacent solar elastosis in the adult form
Management centres on sun protection, avoidance of causative agents, and physical measures such as cryotherapy, dermabrasion or laser for cosmetically troublesome lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Colloid milium is defined by accumulation of amorphous colloid material in the upper dermis, but the origin differs by subtype. In the common adult form, chronic ultraviolet exposure drives severe solar elastosis, and the colloid is thought to derive from actinically degenerated elastic fibres, accumulating as fissured eosinophilic masses in the papillary dermis. The juvenile form, by contrast, appears to arise from filamentous degeneration of epidermal keratinocytes, producing colloid that is immunohistochemically distinct and often keratin-related, closer in nature to the amyloid seen in keratinocyte-derived cutaneous amyloidosis. The pigmented variant reflects colloid deposition associated with topical hydroquinone and shares features with exogenous ochronosis.
additionalDifferentials: Primary cutaneous amyloidosis, especially nodular and macular forms
Solar elastosis with cysts and comedones (Favre-Racouchot)
Milia and eruptive vellus hair cysts
Exogenous ochronosis in the pigmented variant
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating fissured colloid masses in the papillary dermis
Congo red and thioflavin staining to distinguish colloid from amyloid, alongside clinicopathological correlation
Immunohistochemistry to differentiate elastic-derived from keratin-derived colloid where the subtype is unclear
Detailed drug and cosmetic history focused on hydroquinone or skin-lightening product use
Dermoscopy to characterise the amber, structureless papules
Assessment of cumulative photodamage and photoprotection habits
redFlags: Rapid growth, bleeding or ulceration suggesting an alternative neoplastic diagnosis
Widespread or atypical distribution prompting reconsideration of amyloidosis
New pigmented deposits raising concern for ongoing hydroquinone-related ochronosis
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring biopsy to exclude cutaneous malignancy on sun-damaged skin
reference.prognosis: Colloid milium is a benign, largely cosmetic condition; the adult form tends to persist and may slowly progress with continued sun exposure, whereas the juvenile form may stabilise or regress after puberty. There is no risk of systemic involvement, and outcomes are good with photoprotection and, where desired, physical removal.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing colloid as amyloid or vice versa, since both may show subtle overlapping staining and require careful correlation
Overlooking hydroquinone use as a cause of the pigmented variant
Treating aggressively without recognising the benign, purely cosmetic nature of the condition
Failing to reinforce sun protection, allowing the adult form to progress
Assuming solitary amber papules on sun-damaged skin are benign without biopsy when features are atypical
